title: Unbounded GHZ dimension from fixed-order multiphoton sources
problem: High-dimensional GHZ states can be made by entanglement by path identity: coherent sources each emit photons into a fixed set of paths, and one keeps only the events with exactly one photon per path. With two-photon sources the achievable local dimension is at most \(3\), and at most \(2\) on six or more paths, because Bogdanov's theorem limits graphs whose perfect matchings are pairwise edge-disjoint. Krenn and coauthors asked whether three-photon sources can produce GHZ states of arbitrarily large local dimension.
result: Yes. For every source order \(r\ge3\) and every number of paths \(n\) divisible by \(r\), there is a network of \(r\)-photon sources whose postselected state is \(\ket{\mathrm{GHZ}_{n,d}}\) with \(d\ge c_rn^{2(r-2)/7}\); for triplets, \(d\ge(n/384)^{2/7}\). Conversely, every such network has \(d=O_r(n^{r-1}/\log n)\). On nine paths the maximum is exactly \(13\) for unrestricted triplet sources and \(6\) when each source feeds one path in each of three fixed groups.
significance: The answer separates two-photon from multiphoton sources: pair sources are capped at dimension three, while triplet sources are not capped at all. The work turns an experimental design question into the extremal combinatorics of rigid hypergraphs, hypergraphs whose only perfect matchings are a prescribed edge-disjoint family, and settles Krenn's question on this model while confirming the value \(13\) reported by Gu, Chen and Krenn on nine paths.
limitations: The constructions are extremely inefficient: dimension \(12\) needs \(39\) paths in the balanced construction, and the best equal-weight success probability per trial falls from \(3.9\times10^{-4}\) on nine paths to about \(10^{-58}\) on \(117\). The model assumes ideal coherent sources with no which-source information, lossless transmission and perfect photon-number detection, and each source's photons share one internal label. The gap between \(n^{2/7}\) and \(n^2/\log n\) for triplets remains open. The authors state that all proofs were generated by GPT; the principal theorems are formalized in Lean 4 in the authors' public repository.

methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: Represent each output path by a vertex and each source by the set of \(r\) paths it feeds, a hyperedge. The sources that emit in an accepted event must cover every path exactly once, so accepted events are perfect matchings of the hypergraph. If the sources of label \(i\) form a perfect matching \(M_i\), the event in which exactly they emit contributes \(\ket{i}^{\otimes n}\). The postselected state is a GHZ state of dimension \(d\) exactly when \(M_1,\ldots,M_d\) are edge-disjoint and are the only perfect matchings, which the paper calls \(d\)-rigid (Proposition 2.1). Any other matching would contribute a mixed label string.

For pairs, Bogdanov's theorem says that only \(K_4\) has three or more pairwise edge-disjoint perfect matchings with no others, so \(d\le3\). For triples on six paths, all \(20\) triples form \(10\) complementary pairs and give \(d=10\). The difficulty on more paths is that a triple usually extends to a perfect matching in many ways, and the construction must leave each prescribed matching as the only completion of its own triples.

The construction works with three groups \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) of paths. Projected to \(A\times B\), each matching is a cycle cover of a digraph; the third path of each triple is a tag in \(C\) chosen as an anchor plus a translation vector depending on the matching. A mixed choice of triples that still covers \(A\) and \(B\) once must have a different sum of tags, so it misses some path in \(C\). With translations \(\mathbf v_{ab}=(a,b,\binom a2+\binom b2)\) and a digraph called the double comb, this gives \(t^2\) matchings on parts of size \(O(t^7)\). Products of \(r-2\) such factors sharing \(A\) and \(B\) give the exponent \(2(r-2)/7\).

The upper bound uses the fact that in a rigid hypergraph no partial exchange of edges produces a new perfect matching. A random representative from each edge and an exchange digraph that must be acyclic or one long cycle give \(d\beta_m\le m^{r-1}\) in the balanced case, with \(\beta_m\) the smaller of \(m/2\) and the harmonic number. On nine paths this gives \(g_3(3)\le6\), attained by triples on three copies of \(\mathbb F_3\) with \(a+b+c\in\{0,2\}\); a construction on \(\mathbb F_3^2\) with \(13\) matchings and a certificate-based proof that \(14\) is impossible give \(f_3(9)=13\).

methods.technique: Translation tags that expose every mixed matching
methods.explanation: Two prescribed matchings that agree on the first two groups after a few swaps would create a mixed perfect matching. Choosing the third path of each triple by a vector tag turns that combinatorial danger into a linear-algebra condition: every mixed choice changes the sum of tags.
math: Let the projected matchings be cycle covers \(\mathcal P_1,\ldots,\mathcal P_q\) of a digraph, and give the triple above arc \(e\) of cover \(i\) the tag \(\mathbf z_e+\mathbf v_i\), with \(\{\mathbf z_e+\mathbf v_i:e\in\mathcal P_i\}=C\) for each \(i\). Any perfect matching projects to some \(\mathcal P_i\) and uses every tag once, so comparing it with the prescribed matching gives \[\sum_{e\in\mathcal P_i}\bigl(\mathbf v_{j(e)}-\mathbf v_i\bigr)=\mathbf0,\] where \(j(e)\) is the matching from which the triple above \(e\) was taken. If a linear functional has its unique minimum over the translations at \(\mathbf v_i\), every summand is nonnegative under it and vanishes only when \(j(e)=i\) (Lemma 3.3).

For \(t^2\) covers take \(\mathbf v_{ab}=(a,b,\gamma_a+\gamma_b)\) with \(\gamma_j=\binom j2\), and \(\lambda_{ab}(x,y,z)=2z-(2a-1)x-(2b-1)y\). Then \[\lambda_{ab}(\mathbf v_{a'b'}-\mathbf v_{ab})=(a'-a)^2+(b'-b)^2,\] which is positive unless \((a',b')=(a,b)\). Editorial check: the identity holds for all integer \(a,b,a',b'\) from \(0\) to \(5\), and in the nine-path example of Fig. 2 an exhaustive search finds exactly the two prescribed perfect matchings. The remaining work, done in Appendix A, is to choose anchors from a lattice box so that each cover uses every tag exactly once.
methods.transfer: Tagging by vectors with an exposed-point condition is a general way to make a prescribed family of solutions the only solutions of an exact-cover problem, which applies to designing optical networks for other target states and to rigidity questions for matchings in hypergraphs.

methods.technique: Bounding rigid hypergraphs by forbidden partial exchanges
methods.explanation: To show triplet networks cannot be arbitrarily efficient, one needs an upper bound on the number of edge-disjoint perfect matchings that are the only ones. Rigidity forbids replacing part of a matching while keeping the rest, which constrains a natural exchange digraph.
math: For a perfect matching \(M\) with one representative chosen from each edge, draw \(v\to w\) when replacing \(v\) by \(w\) in its edge gives another edge of \(H\). A directed cycle shorter than \(m\) would produce a new perfect matching sharing an edge with \(M\), contradicting rigidity, so the digraph on representatives is acyclic or a single \(m\)-cycle. In either case \(\sum_v1/(1+d^+(v))\ge\beta_m\). Averaging over random representatives and summing over the \(d\) matchings gives, for balanced \(r\)-partite hypergraphs, \[d\,\beta_m\le\bigl|\{e\setminus V_1:e\in H\}\bigr|\le m^{r-1}.\]

For \(m\ge5\), \(\beta_m=\log m+O(1)\), so \(g_r(m)\le(1+o(1))m^{r-1}/\log m\) and, for unrestricted triples, \(f_3(n)=o(n^2)\). At \(m=3\), \(\beta_3=3/2\) gives \(g_3(3)\le9/(3/2)=6\). Editorial check: the \(18\) triples \((a,b,c)\in\mathbb F_3^3\) with \(a+b+c\in\{0,2\}\) have exactly \(6\) perfect matchings, pairwise edge-disjoint, so the bound is attained.
methods.transfer: Exchange-digraph arguments of this kind bound the number of solutions in other uniqueness problems, such as uniquely completable Latin squares or rigid families of codes, wherever any shorter alternating cycle would create a forbidden new solution.
